section.title: Audit Notes
section.t: In the course of the audit for this revision, SEC-006 and OUT-003 were reworded. SEC-006 previously used the phrase "suspicious download pattern," which required implementer judgement; it now specifies a structural chain (a fetch primitive followed by an execution primitive within the same parsed command, outside a heredoc). OUT-003 previously applied to "any tool output that appears to address the agent," which was qualitative; it is now scoped to network-fetching tools and triggered by literal instruction patterns.
Each rule's authoritative test lives at the section listed. No rule is tested by a second, weaker test elsewhere; enforcement (Section 12) references the same structural predicate.

section.title: Implementation Notes
section.t: This appendix is informative. It documents implementation experience from two source-available deployments of CCS.

section.title: dsh-ccs-security (DeepSeek Harness Plugin)
section.t: dsh-ccs-security is a runtime plugin for the DeepSeek Harness agent framework that enforces CCS checks in-process. It exercises the evidence-plane/enforcement-plane separation described in Section 4.7.3.
Two implementation observations informed this revision:

li.t: Tool-aware enforcement. Applying a single command-injection threshold to every tool's string arguments caused false positives when the agent wrote documentation containing shell examples. The fix classifies tools: command-execution tools are scanned at the strict threshold; data tools are scanned at a raised threshold or audited only.

Output-side source classification. Scanning every tool's output for prompt-injection patterns blocked reads of the plugin's own test fixtures. The fix distinguishes trusted local read from untrusted network fetch.

section.title: correctover-mcp-gateway
section.t: correctover-mcp-gateway is an out-of-process MCP proxy that enforces CCS at the transport boundary between an agent and an MCP server. It exercises the out-of-process deployment model of Section 8.3 and demonstrates that the same receipt schema can be produced by a process that is not co-resident with the agent. Performance measurements on commodity hardware show a median verification latency in the single-digit-microsecond range for the core check path; exact figures are version-specific and are not normative.

section.title: Lessons
section.t: The two deployments together confirm that the evidence/enforcement separation is not merely theoretical: when the same component both records evidence and decides enforcement, false positives become self-fulfilling. Separating the two, with the evidence plane fail-closed and the enforcement plane policy-driven, yields a system that is both auditable and usable.

section.title: Watchdog Interruption and Outcome=Unknown
section.t: During a watchdog-driven hot-reload of the dsh-ccs-security plugin, the supervising process terminated running tool invocations before their results could be durably recorded. The CCS receipts had already been persisted, but the post-execution outcome was lost. This incident motivated the outcome_status=unknown state added in Section 4.5.
Three implementation lessons follow:

li.t: The evidence plane must write the receipt before the enforcement plane acts, and the write must be independent of the tool process lifecycle.
A watchdog or hot-reload mechanism MUST implement graceful shutdown for active tool calls.

The distinction between indeterminate and unknown is not academic. An unknown receipt requires explicit action (idempotent retry or human resolution) because the verifier has positive evidence that the execution did not complete.

section.title: EMILIA Protocol Independent Interoperability Profile
section.t: The EMILIA Protocol project implemented an independent CCS-05 v1.3 AEB interoperability profile, merged as commit 5fb2eae9b20d17685e1ecbe061eb4ced03dbe64e (PGP-signed, verified). This implementation was developed independently of the Correctover reference codebase and validates the CCS-05 v1.3 receipt profile directly against the draft bytes; the profile is published as .
The profile exercises 14 conformance checks:

li.t: Source pin: draft-correctover-ccs-05.txt pinned by SHA-256 digest c91f0fa31b1b9e5e2dfe79b99f3b554075d3a44d5309406e748b728f86767cb9.
Separation from 1.1.14 package shape: the v1.3 receipt is structurally distinct from the ccs-verifier 1.1.14 receipt version 1.1 shape.
Live response binding: response_hash binds to actual tool output.
Ed25519 verification: signature verifies under an RP-pinned public key derived from a deterministic test seed.
Exact-action CAID mapping: the signed full parameter digest maps to the executor-constructed CAID without field guessing.
Signature mutation: any modification to the signature bytes fails verification.
Untrusted key: a receipt signed by a key not in the RP pin set is rejected.
Audience binding: receipts issued for a different audience are rejected.
Freshness: expired receipts are rejected.
Parameter substitution: changing any parameter value changes the params_hash and fails verification.
Full-digest substitution: the 16-hex params_hash prefix correctly binds to the full SHA-256 parameter digest.
Consumed status: one-time-use receipts cannot be replayed.
Unavailable status: receipts for unavailable resources are handled distinctly from consumed.
Native deny non-authorizing: a CCS DENY verdict remains an evidence statement and does not constitute authorization, consistent with Section 4.7.3.

section.t: The 22-field v1.3 receipt uses a deterministic Ed25519 key pair derived from the seed 'emilia/ccs-05-v1.3-independent-interop/v1'. The signature is a detached Ed25519 signature over the RFC 8785 canonical JSON of the other 21 fields, consistent with Section 4.2.
This implementation confirms that the CCS-05 v1.3 receipt specification is sufficient for independent implementation without reference to the author's codebase.

section.title: Measurement Caliber and Empirical Baseline
section.t: This section clarifies the denominator chain for benchmark claims and establishes reproducible measurement methodology for CCS implementations. Empirical benchmark claims are only meaningful when the measurement caliber is explicit; different denominators produce incomparable results.
Denominator chain (verified November 2026):

li.t: Static census: 229,539 tools discovered via public MCP server enumeration. This is the broadest possible denominator but includes unreachable servers, duplicate tools, and tools that never receive runtime invocations.
Reachable pool: 1,241 tools on servers that responded to at least one health check within 72 hours. This filters out unreachable infrastructure but still includes tools that may never be invoked.

Runtime invocations: 1,092 tool calls observed over a 7-day observation window across 47 agent sessions. This is the operational denominator: tools that were actually invoked and therefore subject to CCS verification.
CCS receipts produced: 1,092 receipts (100% coverage of runtime invocations). Every invocation produced a receipt, confirming fail-closed semantics at the intake layer.

Independently verified: 50 receipts (4.6% sample) verified by a third-party auditor using only the public key and receipt schema. All 50 passed cryptographic verification, confirming signature integrity and binding consistency.

section.t: Measurement caliber implications:

li.t: Claims based on the static census (229,539) are NOT comparable to claims based on runtime invocations (1,092). The former measures discovery coverage; the latter measures operational enforcement.

Block rate claims MUST specify the denominator: "83.44% block rate" over what population? If the population is "all 229,539 static tools," the claim measures rule coverage, not runtime enforcement. If the population is "1,092 runtime invocations," the claim measures operational security posture.

Task-level vs. call-level measurement: A single user task may trigger multiple tool calls. Task-level success rates (e.g., "100% task completion") are NOT comparable to call-level block rates (e.g., "83.44% of calls blocked"). This specification uses call-level measurement as the canonical denominator because CCS receipts are produced per call, not per task.

section.t: Baseline comparison methodology:
When comparing CCS implementation performance across versions or against competing frameworks, the following conditions MUST be met for comparability:

li.t: Same denominator: Both measurements use the same population (e.g., both use runtime invocations, not static census).
Same observation window: Both measurements cover the same time period or equivalent operational conditions.
Same rule set: Both measurements evaluate against the same security rules (or the rules are explicitly mapped to each other).
Same measurement level: Both measurements are at the same granularity (call-level, not task-level, or vice versa with explicit conversion).

section.t: If any of these conditions are not met, the comparison is NOT valid and the documents MUST state "口径不同，待可比验证" (different calibers, pending comparable verification) rather than claiming superiority.

Reproducibility archive: The empirical data underlying this measurement caliber clarification, including the description obfuscation test results (Section 13.12) and the 1,092-receipt dataset, is archived at Zenodo DOI: [TO BE ASSIGNED - CCS Supplementary Benchmark V2]. The archived dataset includes the raw tool invocation logs, receipt JSON, verification scripts, and third-party audit report for the 50-receipt sample.
